headline: AI giants promise publishers new way to block some scraping
body: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic pledged on Friday to give media outlets and other websites a single way to prevent their content from being scraped to train artificial intelligence (AI) models

OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic pledged on Friday to give media outlets and other websites a single way to prevent their content from being scraped to train artificial intelligence (AI) models, amid growing criticisms and legal battles from news publishers.

Publishers currently have to implement multiple blocking commands for every bot that crawls the web to collect data , but the new proposed solution will allow them to enter a single, standardized instruction that's recognized and honored by any AI company that adopts the protocol.

Microsoft will implement it beginning February 1, 2027, and Google sometime in 2027. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it will roll it out "in the coming months," while Claude-maker Anthropic said it has "already started" rolling it out.

The announcement comes as publishers are facing a surge in bots that scrape their articles to feed AI models. Some, like the New York Times, have taken the matter to court.

In December 2023, the Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft for allegedly using millions of its articles without authorization or payment to train ChatGPT. The two tech companies are invoking an exception to copyright law known as fair use.

Meanwhile, internet infrastructure provider Cloudflare has blocked AI bots by default on new customer sites since July 2025, and a standard called Really Simple Licensing already allows publishers to charge bots that visit their pages.

The story so far: Microsoft has introduced a voluntary exit offer for eligible employees in India , the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada, as the technology giant expands its artificial intelligence (AI) business and changes how work is organised.

In an October 26 announcement, Amy Coleman, Microsoft’s executive vice-president and chief people officer, said the offer would give eligible employees considering leaving the company financial support and career-planning resources. The programme is available to employees in selected teams, with participation depending on business priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs.

The latest offer follows two earlier workforce measures, such as the elimination of around 4,800 roles and a Voluntary Retirement Program in which more than 30% of eligible employees chose to participate. Microsoft has not disclosed how many employees it expects to leave under the new offer.

While the company has not explicitly linked the latest programme to AI-driven job displacement or cost savings, its workforce announcements, financial disclosures and account of its internal AI transformation provide context for the decision.

Microsoft is restructuring even as its business grows. In its fiscal 2026 results, the company reported revenue of $331.8 billion, up 18% from the previous year, and operating income of $155.2 billion, up 21%.

Kamal Karanth, co-founder of specialist staffing firm Xpheno, described Microsoft’s voluntary exit offer (VEO) as “a timely manpower optimisation move” against the backdrop of operational efficiencies achieved over the last four fiscal periods.
